US Alzheimer blood-biomarker ordering rose 6.5-fold in 18 months

Across 35.9 million adults in Epic Cosmos, 69,907 had an Alzheimer blood-biomarker order; quarterly ordering increased from 27.5 to 179.7 per 100,000 active patients, while only about 5% received a new amyloid-PET or CSF order within 90 days.

Key quantitative results: Among 35,900,955 active adults aged at least 50 years, 69,907 (0.19%) had an index Alzheimer blood-biomarker order.

BiomarkersBloodPlasma p-tauPlasma Aβ42/40Real-world implementation

Added November 27, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jama.2026.23534; PMID:43050206; PMCID:PMC13783107

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Blood-biomarker ordering is diffusing rapidly into US practice, primarily among symptomatic adults, but the EHR signal cannot show whether tests were positive, intermediate, or negative—or whether follow-up was appropriate. The low observed rate of new PET or CSF orders may reflect rule-out use, incomplete capture, access barriers, or unconfirmed diagnosis from plasma alone. The study documents implementation scale, not analytical validity or clinical utility.

Study design

Investigators used Epic Cosmos data from 2,358 hospitals and 52,500 clinics. Adults aged 50 years or older with a clinical encounter from January 2025 through June 2026 were screened for a first p-tau or Aβ blood-test order after at least 365 days without prior Alzheimer blood-biomarker testing. Orders were classified as p-tau only, Aβ42/40 only, or both; index orders through June 10, 2026 had 90-day follow-up.

Key quantitative results

  • Among 35,900,955 active adults aged at least 50 years, 69,907 (0.19%) had an index Alzheimer blood-biomarker order.
  • Quarterly ordering increased from 27.5 per 100,000 active patients in Q1 2025 to 179.7 per 100,000 in Q2 2026, a 6.5-fold increase.
  • Orders were p-tau only for 42,713 patients (61.1%), Aβ42/40 only for 7,673 (11.0%), and p-tau plus Aβ for 19,521 (27.9%).
  • Before or on the order date, 17.2% had documented AD, 21.2% non-AD dementia, 57.1% cognitive symptoms without dementia, and 4.6% no documented cognitive diagnosis.
  • Within 90 days, 15.6% received a newly documented AD diagnosis, approximately 5% had a new amyloid-PET or CSF order, and 63 patients (0.1%) started an anti-amyloid therapy.
  • Neurologists accounted for 51.6% of orders with known ordering specialty; 83.4% of tested patients lived in metropolitan areas.

What changed

Full numerical results now make it possible to quantify how quickly blood-biomarker testing is entering US practice and how infrequently confirmatory testing or anti-amyloid treatment is visible within 90 days.

Strength of evidence

Strong descriptive evidence for EHR-recorded ordering across a very large US network, but low for appropriateness or utility because the study lacked test results, assay identity, clinical rationale, insurance data, and complete capture of external testing and treatment.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Rapid uptake heightens the need for assay-specific interpretation, explicit indeterminate pathways, and documentation of whether positive or intermediate results receive confirmatory PET or CSF testing when required. The study cannot determine whether the observed follow-up was appropriate.

Field medical relevance

Provides the first large-scale implementation baseline for US blood-biomarker use and exposes major measurement gaps between ordering, result interpretation, confirmatory testing, and treatment access.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study used CPT-coded orders and could not identify assay brand, result category, or analytical performance. It measures implementation and downstream care, not test validity.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Testing was concentrated in metropolitan settings and only 42.9% of tested patients had Medicare coverage recorded. The study does not establish payer coverage or explain whether access barriers contributed to low observed confirmatory testing and treatment.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does the study show that clinicians are skipping confirmatory testing?
No. Test results and clinical rationale were unavailable, and external PET, CSF, or referrals may not be captured. The approximately 5% rate is an implementation signal, not proof of inappropriate care.
Can these data compare individual blood assays?
No. CPT-coded orders did not identify assay brand or result category.
Does rapid ordering establish clinical utility?
No. Uptake is separate from analytical validity, diagnostic accuracy, improved decisions, patient outcomes, authorization, and coverage.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Orders rather than completed tests or results
  • No assay brand, cutoffs, or positive/intermediate/negative categories
  • No clinical rationale, insurance-coverage detail, or assessment of appropriateness
  • External tests, referrals, and treatments may be incompletely captured
  • Only 90 days of post-order follow-up
  • CPT coding may misclassify or miss blood-biomarker testing

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Fu M, Andersen M, Ramachandran R, Berg KM, Ross JS. Blood-Based Biomarker Testing for Alzheimer Disease in US Clinical Practice. JAMA. Published online November 18, 2026. doi:10.1001/jama.2026.23534.
